www.nba.com/news/power-r...

images.alt:
It’s fair to say that the Spurs should have won the championship four months ago. They led all five games of the Finals by at least 12 points, and made a couple of brutal mistakes in the closing seconds of Games 2 and 4. With Victor Wembanyama, Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper just 22, 21 and 20 years old, respectively, there should be many more opportunities ahead, and the next chapter starts now.

Preseason takeaways

Castle, Harper and De’Aaron Fox played just 73 total minutes (regular season, NBA Cup final and playoffs combined) together last season, and the Spurs were outscored by 26.1 points per 100 possessions (scoring an anemic 84.6 per 100) in those minutes. But that’s the way they’re going to start the season, with Wembanyama and Devin Vassell rounding out the starting lineup. The three guards played in the final two preseason games together, and the Spurs outscored the Suns and Kings by 27 points (scoring 68 on 54 offensive possessions) in a little less than 23 minutes with all three on the floor.

Wembanyama shot just 1-for-12 from 3-point range, but 26 (60%) of his 43 shots came in the paint. That was up from 50% last season and 57% in the playoffs.

Something to watch in Week 1: The possession game. When you play the Thunder, you have to take care of the ball. When you play the Rockets, you have to protect the defensive glass. The Spurs won the possession game in eight of their 16 games against Oklahoma City and Houston last season, and they’ll host them both this week.

Memphis Grizzlies OVER 29.5 
The 25-26 Grizzlies were one of the easiest fade calls I’ve ever had doing this. Between Ja Morant struggling to stay healthy and trading away Desmond Bane for picks, it was easy to call a step back. After Zach Edey got hurt in early December after just 11 games, the season was over. 
Soon after Edey went down, they traded away Jaren Jackson Jr. to Utah and shut Morant down for a one-year tank. They executed it masterfully and got the luck they needed, landing Cam Boozer in the draft. Boozer, Edey, Cedric Coward and the NBA’s new anti-tanking rules are all big reasons why I believe 30 wins is more than reasonable for this Grizzlies team.

Miami Heat OVER 45.5 - SUPER PICK 
I feel like everybody is trying to outsmart themselves a little too much when it comes to the Miami Heat. Yes, they were the 10-seed and lost in the Play-In last year. And yes, it’s also true that they don’t have big names in their prime to provide elite shooting around Giannis and Bam Adebayo. But the overemphasis on shooting, a skill that can be found in 2026 for relatively cheap, while overlooking having two of the league’s best big men makes me feel like I’m going a little insane. 
The last two NBA Champions won the title by playing significant portions of the game with two 7-footers on the court and dominating the offensive boards. The front office jargon du jour calls this “winning the possession game.” The other way to say it: rebounding and size win basketball games, the same as it ever has been since the days of Mikan. So if the possession game is en vogue, and the Heat have two elite in-their-prime big men, the conventional wisdom is they’re going to be an average team??? Give me a break!

Oklahoma City Thunder UNDER 62.5 - SUPER PICK 
Let me start by saying that Oklahoma City will be, at worst, the 2nd best team in the West. But they are feeling the impact of the new CBA, even as the league’s example franchise. Thanks to major money extensions for key members of their 2025 NBA Championship team, the Thunder had to make tough choices, sending away several members of that title team for basically nothing in return, hoping to backfill them NFL-style with draft picks. 
Defensive tone-setter Lu Dort and bucket-getting guard Aaron Wiggins were shipped to Atlanta. Dort, a fellow Canadian like MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, was one of SGA’s best friends on the team and one of the pillars of the team’s physical defense-first identity. Sharpshooter Isaiah Joe got sent to Detroit. The Thunder will try to replace those lost minutes with more Olivia Dean TikToks and stepback 3s from Jared McCain, an increased role for last year’s breakout star Ajay Mitchell, and more minutes for two-way stud Cason Wallace. They also drafted Transfer Portal legend Bennett Stirtz, who rose from Division II to the first round. They also drafted Kentucky guard Otega Oweh, who suffered a torn Achilles and won’t be a factor this season.

Portland Trail Blazers OVER 40.5 
Setting aside Lillard’s homecoming last summer, Ja Morant is the most famous Blazer to join the team since the team signed Carmelo Anthony in 2019. Unlike the Anthony move, months later, the Morant move is still a head-scratcher for a team lacking wing depth after sending Jerami Grant to Memphis. The further away we get from the move, the more it looks like a hasty move by a new owner who didn’t believe that at 36 years old, coming off an Achilles tear, Damian Lillard would still be Damian Lillard. images.alt:
Utah Jazz UNDER 36.5 
In the summer, I was a bit of a Utah Jazz Hipster. After drafting Darryn Peterson and watching him cook in Summer League, I was ready to ride the bandwagon. But then the Summer League glow wore off, the weather got colder, and I started to look more critically at the Jazz. I’m not sure I can join the dirty soda and Crumbl cookie party. 
This team has a lot of guard talent, not unlike the Blazers. Jusuf Nurkic has found a home in Utah, which is great for a guy who looked like he’d be out of the league not long ago. But that underscores the biggest problem I have with the Jazz: I’m not sold on their big men.
Jaren Jackson Jr. is a great shot blocker, has great 3-point range, and Lauri Markkanen is a great scorer. But feel free to call me Unc: seven-footers who can’t rebound well aren’t the kind of seven-footers I’d like to employ. More than ever in today’s NBA, REBOUNDING MATTERS. The Jazz will rotate Nurkic, Jaxson Hayes and Kyle Filipowski next to Markkanen and Jackson and I just don’t love that combo of big men. Did I mention they also have Mo Bamba? It’s a weird big man room and not one that I think will win them enough games to beat this projection.

How many games until team stats actually mean something?

Thanks to research by @knarsu3.bsky.social this chart shows when each stat starts to stabilize and become reliable. After one game, everything’s noise!

I’ll update you throughout the season to show which stats we can actually start trusting.

images.alt: Chart titled "# of games until we can trust team stats." Horizontal bars show roughly when each NBA team stat becomes reliable, by game number. Earliest to stabilize, around games 4 to 9: pace, three-point attempt rate, free throw rate and assist percentage. Middle range, games 7 to 20: opponent three-point attempt rate, win percentage, net rating, turnover percentage, two-point percentage, offensive rebound percentage, true shooting percentage, offensive rating, opponent free throw rate, defensive rebound percentage and opponent turnover percentage. Free throw percentage and defensive rating settle around games 16 to 21. Three-point percentage takes longest, around games 27 to 30. Research by Krishna Narsu, posted to Nylon Calculus.
